    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session.
    • Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review.
    • In a recent development, on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session. It also decided an interim docket case on border wall construction in southwestern Texas, granting the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to continue construction in an apparent 8-1 vote.

    Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    In a recent development, on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew. Just over an hour later, Pavatt was executed in Oklahoma.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    On Monday, the justices heard argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Sources indicate that also on Monday, the justices heard argument in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Industry observers note that later on Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

    Industry observers note that in Monday’s order list, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists.

    Recent findings suggest that in early October, a high school wrestler in Washington state and her mother came to the Supreme Court’s interim docket and asked the justices to prevent transgender girls from competing against her during this year’s wrestling season. The application has been fully briefed since Oct. 15, but the Supreme Court has not yet taken action. In a Monday letter, the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association asked the court not to intervene, highlighting the passage last week of a ballot initiative in Washington that aims to prevent “biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities that have separate classifications for male and female students” at K-12 schools.

    It has been revealed that while speaking to the Federalist Society on Thursday, Justice Samuel Alito “warned against any potential congressional action to defund the Supreme Court as he defended the importance of an independent judiciary,” according to The Hill. “Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities,” he said. “So, it is crucial to preserve the independence of the judiciary. If that is eliminated, then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.” He also described the judicial branch as “the least powerful branch,” adding that “it is ‘vulnerable’ to Congress and the executive.” But that doesn’t mean judges can’t go too far, Alito added. “If you think about a hand grenade, a 500-pound bomb and a nuclear weapon,” he said, “the hand grenade is the least dangerous. But that is not to say that it is not dangerous.”.

    In a recent development, in February, “the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Donald Trump imposed last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act,” holding that the law does not grant the president the power to impose tariffs. The next month, the U.S. Court of International Trade “ordered Customs and Border Patrol to problem refunds to importers totaling about $166 billion.” Now, seven Senate Democrats are asking the Federal Trade Commission “to investigate whether large corporations that received billions of dollars in tariff refunds violated federal law by not passing them on to their customers,” according to USA Today. “By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs,” the senators wrote, “corporations may be in violation of the” Federal Trade Commission Act, which “empowers the commission to prevent ‘unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.’”.

    Sources indicate that during a Thursday panel at the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Convention, “White House counsel Will Scharf praised the Supreme Court’s June decision strengthening presidential firing power as a ‘generational win’” that “righted what he viewed as a ‘historic constitutional wrong,’” according to The Hill. “A president who can’t control who’s exercising the executive power that is vested in him, that’s a cabined presidency,” Scharf said. “The Supreme Court did a masterful job,” he added. “Really got it right.”.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday, former death row inmate Richard Glossip appeared in Oklahoma County District Court “for what was supposed to be his second hearing on pretrial motions” in the state’s effort to retry him for the 1997 murder of Barry Van Treese. “However, the hearing took a turn when the state announced an agreement between the prosecution and the defense,” under which “Glossip pleaded guilty to one count of accessory to murder,” according to KOKH in Oklahoma City. The plea agreement comes after the Supreme Court in 2025 “threw out Glossip’s murder conviction and death sentence,” determining that prosecutors had failed to correct false testimony. “Glossip’s sentencing is set for Dec. 17 and Dec. 18.”.

    Adam Liptak, The New York Times.

    It has been revealed that in his newsletter for The Newly introduced York Times, Adam Liptak highlighted “hurdles and roadblocks [] erected by the Supreme Court” that may stand in the way of at least some of the new Congress’ planned investigations into “the Trump administration and its allies.” For example, in 2024’s Trump v. United States, in which the court granted the president “substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.” “Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding ‘which crimes to investigate and prosecute.’” It is also significant, according to Liptak, that “the court has never definitively resolved” whether Congress can “sue the executive branch,” an matter that will likely arise if the administration refuses “to give Congress documents or let officials testify.” Liptak noted that “it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate” disputes between Congress and the executive branch over access to information, “or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.”.

    Sources indicate that during the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats in cases on birthright citizenship, tariffs, and his effort to fire Lisa Cook. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those challenges.

    Recent findings suggest that in his Nuts and Bolts column, Stephen Wermiel explored how the Supreme Court decides what cases to decide, also known as the certiorari or “cert.” process. According to him, “questions will continue to arise about how th[is] process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.”.

    In a column for SCOTUSblog, Deborah Hellman and Lily Hu revisited the Supreme Court’s decision to grant review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on the circumstances under which facially neutral admissions policies violate equal protection by producing a discriminatory effect.

    In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored 11 petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices during today’s conference, which cover such problems as the Trump administration’s effort to remove certain noncitizens from the country without first allowing them to apply for asylum and a ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    In his Born Free and Equal column on Wednesday, Steven Calabresi reviewed Justice Samuel Alito’s new book and commended it as “exceptionally intellectual and provocative.” “The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not,” Calabresi concluded.

    On Tuesday, Amy reported that the Trump administration has once again asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to build a newly introduced White House ballroom. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in her inaugural Substance and Procedure column on Monday, Rachel Bayefsky explored the Supreme Court’s application of a “history-and-tradition” analysis in recent cases on the constitutionality of agency adjudication – that is, “the practice of resolving disputes ‘in-house’ within administrative agencies instead of addressing” them in a court. According to Bayefsky, the court’s decision in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards “may have an crucial impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French analyze free speech concerns from the past three election cycles, including Donald Trump’s “they/them” ad in 2024 and the Trump administration’s threats to social media companies. They then discuss a free speech fight that may define the next two years.

    The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Samuel Nelson, who served on the court from 1845 to 1872.

    While you might think there’s only one justice with the name Samuel based on recent news coverage, there have actually been five with that first name in the court’s history – and in today’s justice biography, we’ll take a look at the second. (The first, if you recall, didn’t get things off to a particularly great start: He is the only justice to have been impeached.).

    Recent findings suggest that although referred to as “one of those nineteenth-century justices of whom we often lose sight” (the Journal of Supreme Court History said it, not us), Justice Samuel Nelson served on the court for 27 years as a “pragmatic yet low-key man,” as described by Oyez. Things began for him in Hebron, Latest York, where he was born in November 1792 to Scot-Irish farmers. His father helped pay Nelson’s Middlebury College tuition by selling a person who was enslaved. Nelson graduated from Middlebury in 1813; clerked at a Salem law firm; followed one of its partners to Madison County, New York when the firm split; and was admitted to the bar in 1817 (two years later, he married his law firm practice partner’s daughter).

    According to recent reports, in 1820, Nelson was appointed the town’s postmaster and served as a presidential elector for James Monroe. He became a delegate to the 1821 state constitutional convention, where he pushed to eliminate property requirements for male voters.

    New York Gov. Joseph Yates appointed Nelson as a state circuit judge in 1823. Gov. Enos Throop elevated him to the New York Supreme Court of Judicature (that state’s highest trial court) in 1831, and he became its chief justice in 1837. In Jack v. Martin, he held that New York could not interfere with enforcement of the federal Fugitive Slave Act and noted that anyone who seized a free man would, under state law, “be answerable like any other trespasser or kidnapper.”.

    According to recent reports, in 1845, Nelson ran for the U.S. Senate and lost. Shortly after, President John Tyler nominated him to succeed Justice Smith Thompson. The Senate confirmed Nelson by voice vote in February 1845, and he served as circuit justice for the 2nd Circuit (Connecticut, New York, and Vermont) while on the Supreme Court.

    On the bench, Nelson “kept a low profile,” generally voting with the majority. He did write a few notable decisions, one of them in 1850’s Hotchkiss v. Greenwood, a landmark patent law case. In 1857’s Fellows v. Blacksmith, Nelson wrote for a unanimous court that a land tech giant could not forcibly evict the Tonawanda Senecas, calling such litigation “appalling.” According to one scholar, Nelson “persuaded all his brethren, including those who had supported Jacksonian Indian removal policies, of the merits of the Tonawandas’ Seneca treaty arguments.” The same scholar wrote that Fellows eventually allowed for the treaty that let the tribe buy back 7,500 acres of its reservation.

    Fellows was decided the same year as Dred Scott v. Sandford. Nelson reportedly resisted behind-the-scenes pressure from incoming President James Buchanan to endorse at least part of Chief Justice Roger Taney’s opinion (unlike Justice Robert Grier). Nevertheless, he concurred with the majority, and scholars have “castigat[ed] him, along with Justice Robert Grier of Pennsylvania, for being the only two Northern jurists on the bench who voted with the majority in the case.” (Ten years later in Georgia v. Stanton, Nelson refused to let Georgia block Congress’ Reconstruction program, holding that its claims “call for the judgment of the court upon political questions.”).

    In the lead-up to the Civil War, Nelson and Justice John Campbell acted as intermediaries between Secretary of State William Seward and Southern commissioners who wanted the Confederacy recognized. Privately, Nelson wrote on Christmas Day in 1860 that “we almost despair of the republic” and in 1862 wrote to Justice Benjamin Curtis that he hoped the country might survive both “the fierceness of the enemy without and imbecility of the authorities within.”.

    According to recent reports, nelson also dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not legally blockade Southern ports until Congress declared war. The dissent (along with his vote in Ex parte Milligan to overturn the conviction of a man charged with helping the Confederacy and opposing expanding federal power) led critics to question his loyalty to the Union.

    It has been revealed that following the civil war, President Ulysses S. Grant in 1871 named the 79-year-old Nelson one of five American members of the commission handling claims against Great Britain for the damages caused by British-built Confederate ships, which Nelson accepted (although he wrote that he was “hardly at liberty to refuse”). The proceedings won the United States $15.5 million.

    Recent findings suggest that nelson retired in November 1872. He died in Cooperstown, New York, in December 1873, at age 81. One historian wrote that Nelson was a “quietly competent jurist” in comparison to several of “his more flamboyant and controversial judicial brethren” (some of whom we will be covering soon).

    According to recent reports, on Nov. 10, Judge Richard Posner passed away at the age of 87. Posner, who served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit from 1981 to 2017, was one of the most influential jurists never to have served on the Supreme Court. In addition to his voluminous opinions (some affirmed, others denied), Posner authored over 60 books and more than 500 articles and served as a Senior Lecturer in Law at the University of Chicago Law School. Among his many contributions, Posner helped give life to the law and economics movement and to the study of judging as an empirical pursuit. As Zach, our executive editor, can attest to first-hand, he was both charming and hilarious in person and did not suffer bad ideas lightly. But this is SCOTUSblog. So what did Posner have to say about the court specifically? Here are some choice quotations (you may notice a theme):.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006.
    • Sources indicate that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S.
    • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    Sources indicate that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia said Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    #78837. Tech Report: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that one of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights.
    • Recent findings suggest that before the court is a petition to review the U.S.
    • According to recent reports, though the pipeline manufacturer is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the problem to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that one of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock), Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “atmosphere” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

    Recent findings suggest that before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline company. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

    According to recent reports, though the pipeline manufacturer is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the problem to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in Oneida County v. Oneida Indian Nation, which held that there is a federal common law cause of action allowing Indigenous property owners to bring trespass actions in federal court.

    The Andeavor case has been accompanied in recent years by a slate of lower court decisions similarly diminishing Indigenous property rights. In Davilla v. Enable Midstream Partners, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit held that a pipeline trespasser on Indigenous property would not be ordered to remove the pipeline until the federal district court decided it was, among other things, in the “public interest” to do so. Under federal law, federal courts may not order injunctive relief unless such relief is in the public interest. The 10th Circuit’s decision imposed a public interest standard on Indigenous property when, arguably, it would not have done so in relation to private property.

    Similarly, a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin held in Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe Indians v. Enbridge Inc. that the tribe was not entitled to the immediate removal of a trespassing pipeline because the public interest favored its continued operation. Fortunately, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit reversed that decision. Other federal courts have also ordered immediate eviction of trespassers to Indigenous lands (e.g., United States v. Osage Wind), but the judiciary tends to invoke the public interest when favoring pipeline or other petroleum industry companies.

    Newland argues that some judges may be channeling a long tradition where the federal government assumed that Indigenous property is public property: Most pipelines running through Indigenous lands now originated in an earlier era where the federal government assumed a kind of guardianship over tribal nations, where the Interior Department granted easements and rights-of-way over Indigenous lands without tribal consent. For example, the Supreme Court once held that the secretary of the Interior was empowered to issue leases to natural resources extraction companies even over tribal opposition (Cherokee Nation v. Hitchcock).

    Recent findings suggest that the tradition of guardianship arose in early Supreme Court decisions comparing the federal-tribal relationship to a “guardian-ward” relationship (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia). Congress did not enact laws generally asserting actual guardianship over tribal nations; instead, the relationship was more accurately characterized as a trust relationship, with federal government owning and managing tribal and individual Indian asserts in trust.

    A trust beneficiary has legal rights that a ward does not. A ward does not possess the legal capacity to make their own decisions, while tribal nations and tribal citizens do. When federal or state actors did assert guardianship over Indigenous assets, tragedy often followed, as evidenced in the early 20th century killings of Osage people fictionalized in the film “Killers of the Flower Moon” or in the flooding of several Indian reservations in the mid-20th century by federal hydroelectric dam projects.

    Sources indicate that often, when tribal nations attempted to assert their own legal rights, the judiciary allowed the federal government to block those efforts. Justice Neil Gorsuch recently raised this problem in his dissent in Arizona v. Navajo Nation, where he pointed out that, decades ago, the federal government blocked the Navajo Nation from asserting their water rights, which remain unsettled to this day. In those older cases, the fact that the federal government could stand in the shoes of Indigenous interests suggested that Indigenous property was therefore, in effect, public property.

    It has been revealed that the Department of Justice’s litigation positions also frequently hearken back to expansive federal controls over Indigenous property. While the Supreme Court has explicitly overturned the earlier cases analogizing the federal-tribal relationship as a guardianship in cases such as United States v. Sioux Nation, DOJ attorneys are known to continue to assert guardianship-type control over Indigenous property. Indeed, federal judges have sanctioned them for making such claims post-Sioux Nation.

    This legacy of guardianship once again has raised its head. D.C. Circuit briefing has concluded in a claim brought by the Tohono O’Odham Nation against the Department of Homeland Security regarding the administration’s proposal to build a border wall on the tribe’s land. The tribe argues that the federal common law cause of action recognized in Oneida undergirds the suit. In response, the DOJ now asserts that tribal nations may not sue the United States for trespass on hands held in trust by the federal government for the benefit of a tribal nation. This claim rings again of guardianship, where a ward normally does not have the legal capacity to sue their guardian.

    The import of the government’s claim in the border wall case, like the trespass action in Andeavor, has enormous consequences for Indian country: If the government can confiscate Indigenous property held in trust by the United States, then the judiciary will have allowed the federal government to reassume a guardianship-type relationship regardless of tribal consent or the federal government’s trust duties.

    Matthew L.M. Fletcher is the Harry Burns Hutchins Collegiate Professor of Law at the University of Michigan Law School.

    Recommended Citation: Matthew L.M. Fletcher, Tribal property and the Supreme Court, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 13, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/tribal-property-and-the-supreme-court/.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it.
    • Just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases.
    • Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    As the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it. There are important disputes tied to climate change, immigration, and the Second Amendment. But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs, birthright citizenship, executive authority, and the Voting Rights Act.

    Just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases. Perhaps of even greater note, though, is that it’s short on cases in general, as the court is running behind its typical pace for grants.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution for defrauding the law firm through fictitious companies and ‌false settlement claims.

    It has been revealed that prosecutors have alleged that Swett profited for years ⁠by creating fictitious legal services companies that received reimbursements from Motley Rice. In addition, he allegedly filed fake personal injury claims for family members and put the proceeds into bank accounts that he controlled.

    #78823. Industry News: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1569 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border.
    • The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.
    • Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

    The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

    Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

    The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be promptly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

    Sources indicate that the challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

    In a recent development, U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

    According to recent reports, A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

    Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”.

    Sources indicate that the D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

    It has been revealed that contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most vital and effective pieces of the President’s response.”.

    Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he mentioned, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”.

    In a recent development, sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”.

    And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent plans to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”.

    Sources indicate that the challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a fresh removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”.

    The statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”.

    Sources indicate that the challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they remarked, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

    The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

    In a recent development, the court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services manufacturer violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

    The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

    The investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors stated, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”.

    Industry observers note that in a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the tech giant’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”.

    The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 11:34 am CST.

    It has been revealed that david Beckham poses after he was made a knight bachelor at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle on Nov. 4, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Photo by Andrew Matthews/Getty Images).

    A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a Upcoming York court to dismiss the case.

    The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the Newly introduced York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another tech giant.

    DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

    According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

    Sources indicate that “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint said. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

    According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

    Coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent firm, declined to comment to the AP.

    Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

    According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justice Pierce Butler, who served on the Supreme Court from 1923 to 1939, died on this day in 1939. Butler was the first Minnesotan appointed to the Supreme Court and the only dissenter in the infamous case of Buck v. Bell (though he did not write anything).

    On Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, they announced that they had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, a dispute over whether a financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering. For more on these cases, see the On Site section below.

    Additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    The December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.

    • A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.
    • Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    According to recent reports, “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law noted. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    According to recent reports, A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    #78807. Tech Report: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1326 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move swiftly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    For most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Industry observers note that against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    It has been revealed that the court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    But I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    Another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    In a recent development, that leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    Recent findings suggest that alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    As I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    The administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    Pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    Industry observers note that the 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    Alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the new term.

    The 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    So Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the issue-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    It has been revealed that dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    Recommended Citation: Taraleigh Davis, “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/im-afraid-this-is-going-to-continue-justice-alito-the-executive-and-the-emergency-docket/.

    #78802. Latest Update: Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1850 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    According to recent reports, originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    It has been revealed that for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    According to recent reports, similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    For example, the founding generation did not disarm casual consumers of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    Industry observers note that if the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    Industry observers note that this criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Finally, and most important in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    It has been revealed that sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    It has been revealed that recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    Bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Sources indicate that many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    From an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Sources indicate that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky claims, courts must decide: which tradition?

    The existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at issue in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    #78799. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1265 w)

    Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, by Scott A.
    • For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
    • Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, by Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

    For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

    Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

    The profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

    When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

    The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

    The ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

    That guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train owners and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

    It has been revealed that METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading consumers about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

    Accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

    Final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

    According to recent reports, A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

    Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

    Sources indicate that if a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers upgrade continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

    According to recent reports, five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

    Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

    Industry observers note that ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

    In a recent development, fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

    In a recent development, scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

    In a recent development, editor’s Note: In preparing the content, the authors used generative AI tools under their direction and supervision and provide the following description of the manner and extent of that use. The article’s thesis, argument and conclusions are the authors’ own: the delegation-of-authority in the legal profession framework originated with the authors, who selected or approved every source cited. Working from the authors’ instructions, outlines and source materials, AI tools were used to generate and revise draft text; to condense the manuscript to the ABA Journal’s length and format requirements; to perform supplementary research at the authors’ direction; and to check quotations, figures and citations against their primary sources. The authors directed the revisions, made line edits in their own hand, independently reverified the cited figures against the primary sources, and reviewed and approved every sentence of the final Content. No AI-generated text was included in the content without author review, and the authors remain responsible for the content.

    Mind Your Business is a series of columns written by lawyers, legal professionals and others within the legal industry. The purpose of these columns is to offer practical guidance for attorneys on how to run their practices, provide information about the latest trends in legal technology and how it can help lawyers work more efficiently, and strategies for building a thriving business.
